title: The future of netting and returning
excerpt: In addition to the reduction of the netting scheme, there will be costs for the return of solar power. Read here about the future of netting and return.
contentHtml:
In addition to the planned phasing out of the netting scheme, there will now also be costs for the return of solar power. In this blog we explain what this can mean for you and what the future of netting and returning will look like.

The history of netting.

Solar panels are an excellent way for households to make them more sustainable by converting energy from the sun into electricity. As a result, less energy from the electricity grid is required, which is largely produced with fossil fuels. For a long time, however, solar panels were too expensive for many people. In 2004, the netting scheme was therefore introduced in the Netherlands to make solar panels more attractive for small consumers. This regulation means that electricity surpluses are settled on an annual basis with electricity supplied from the grid. The daily idle power is returned to the grid to make it available to other users. If a household returns more power per year than it receives, users will receive an additional fee on the difference. This compensation differs per energy supplier, and is worth less per kWh than netting. But what does the future of salting and returning look like now?

The finishing of netting.

The netting scheme has significantly improved the demand for solar panels, but it has also created some drawbacks. After all, energy companies incur additional costs by netting, and charge these costs to their customers who do not have solar panels. Thus, people without solar panels have a disadvantage in the solar panels of others. For this reason, the Dutch government has plans to phase out the netting scheme step by step in the period 2025 to 2031. As of 2025, only 64% of generated electricity may be netted, and from 2031, netting is no longer possible. There will still be a fee for electricity supplied to the grid. However, it seems that the return of power will become less favorable.

Source: National government

Charge costs for return power.

Although most energy suppliers offer compensation for the return of electricity, the supplier Vandebron will change this. Vandebron will also charge costs for returning electricity. This is intended to reduce pressure on customers without solar panels, making costs fairer for all customers. In addition, it helps to prevent net congestion by making people return less.

The costs mentioned depend on the amount of electricity that is returned gross. With an annual return up to 5 kWh, there are no costs. If more than 5 kWh is returned annually, fixed delivery costs are charged in scales. Scale 1, for example, is from 5 to 1000 kWh, and has a delivery cost of € 0.13 per day. [1] From 1000 kWh this becomes € 0.41 per day. Customers who return electricity still receive compensation for this, but the daily additional costs reduce their profit. For now, Vandebron is the only supplier to use this system, but it is not unlikely that other energy suppliers will take similar measures.

Source: Vandebron

What to do without returning?

It is of course not nice for customers with solar panels from Vandebron that delivery back will yield less. Yet it is also understandable, because customers without solar panels are less affected in this way and the grid will hopefully become less overloaded. The best tip for users of solar panels is therefore to improve their own use. The Solyx WaterAccu can help with this. This system uses idle solar power to heat tap water. This not only ensures better use of its own solar energy, it also saves gas that is usually used for heating tap water. So if a home battery is not financially feasible, the WaterAccu can still make a profit with your solar power.
